title: Omega-3 fatty acids reprogram tumor-associated macrophage cytokine signaling and suppress pancreatic cancer growth.
abstract: Dietary polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) shape inflammatory signaling within the pancreatic tumor microenvironment (TME), but the cellular mechanisms underlying their effects on tumor progression remain unclear. Using orthotopic models of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), we show that omega-3 (n-3) and omega-6 (n-6) PUFAs are differentially incorporated into tumor lipid pools, generating spatially heterogeneous lipid microenvironments. While an n-6-enriched diet accelerated PDAC growth, an n-3-enriched diet suppressed tumor growth in a T cell-independent manner. Examining inflammatory effects in PDAC tumors, the n-3 PUFA-enriched diet reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines, including IL-6 family members, and single-cell and spatial analyses identified tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) as the primary diet-responsive population. Indeed, selective conversion of n-6 to n-3 fatty acids within myeloid cells using an inducible fat-1 transgene, which encodes an n-3 desaturase that converts n-6 to n-3 PUFAs in vivo, was sufficient to suppress tumor growth, whereas fibroblast-restricted conversion had no effect. This finding is the first to formally establish that cellular origin of PUFA metabolism within the TME is a key determinant of tumor progression and identifies TAMs as critical mediators of n-3-dependent tumor suppression. Furthermore, the n-3 PUFA-enriched diet reduced Arg1+ immunosuppressive TAMs and promoted C1q+ and MHC-II+ antigen-presenting TAM populations enriched for antigen processing machinery and T cell-recruiting chemokines, alongside reduced IL-6 family cytokine production. Together, these findings establish macrophages as key mediators of n-3-driven tumor control and define a mechanism by which dietary lipids remodel cytokine signaling in the PDAC microenvironment.
journal: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America

title: Radiotherapy combined with serplulimab, and chemotherapy as first-line treatment for metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma: a multicenter, single-arm, phase II trial.
abstract:
PURPOSE: The prognosis for metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (mPDAC) remains dismal. In this multicenter, single-arm, phase II study, we evaluated the combination of serplulimab, gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel, and radiotherapy (ICSBR regimen) as first-line treatment for mPDAC patients (ChiCTR2300073237).
METHODS: Patients with mPDAC were enrolled in the first-line setting. The treatment regimen consisted of serplulimab and gemcitabine plus nab-paclitaxel administered in 21-day cycles, combined with stereotactic body radiotherapy directed at the primary or metastatic sites during cycle 2. Additionally, comprehensive biomarker analysis was conducted. The primary endpoint was the 6-month progression-free survival (PFS) rate, with a predefined target of 60%.
RESULT: Forty-six patients received at least one dose of treatment. The 6-month PFS rate was 78.3% (95% CI, 67.2%-91.1%). The median PFS and overall survival (OS) were 8.5 months (95% CI, 7.3-12.0 months) and 14.0 months (95% CI, 12.0 months-not reached), respectively. The objective response rate was 73.9% (95% CI, 58.9%-85.7%). The combination treatment was well tolerated, and no treatment-related deaths or unexpected safety signals were observed. Notably, patients with baseline ctDNA negativity achieved a better survival. Moreover, tumor microenvironment (TME) analysis revealed that baseline fibroblast activation protein-positive cancer-associated fibroblast and T-cell proportions in tumor tissue correlated with clinical outcomes, with distinct spatial distribution and interaction tendencies observed among patients with different responses.
CONCLUSION: Overall, the ICSBR regimen demonstrated a promising survival benefit as first-line treatment for mPDAC. Furthermore, ctDNA status and TME analysis highlighted potential markers for guiding precision treatment.
journal: Clinical cancer research : an official journal of the American Association for Cancer Research

title: Thoracic Pathologies Requiring Surgical or Interventional Management in Solid-Organ Transplant Recipients.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: Thoracic pathologies are important causes of morbidity in solid-organ transplant recipients because of chronic immunosuppression, transplant-related complications, and diverse underlying etiologies. We aimed to evaluate thoracic pathologies requiring surgical or interventional management after solid-organ transplantation, present our clinical outcomes, and propose an anatomical management framework for these complex conditions.
MATERIALS AND METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study at a tertiary referral center of solid-organ transplant recipients who underwent surgical or interventional treatment for thoracic pathologies between 2010 and 2025. Patients who were managed conservatively or patients who had incomplete clinical data were excluded. Demographic characteristics, transplant-related variables, thoracic pathology type, surgical or interventional procedures, histopathological findings, postoperative complications, and clinical outcomes were analyzed descriptively.
RESULTS: Twenty-one transplant recipients underwent 28 thoracic interventions during the study period. The cohort included 12 liver, 8 kidney, and 1 heart transplant recipient, with a mean age of 42.0 ± 22.2 years; 66.7% were male. Thoracic pathologies involved pleural, parenchymal, and mediastinal compartments and required individualized management using tube thoracostomy, video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery, thoracotomy, or mediastinoscopy. Histopathological evaluation demonstrated a broad spectrum of infectious, inflammatory, and malignant diseases, including aspergilloma, tuberculosis, primary lung carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma metastasis, inflammatory pseudotumor, and polymorphic post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease. Postoperative complications occurred in 2 patients (9.5% ). One patient required 2 subsequent thoracotomies for prolonged air leak caused by a parenchymal fistula and postoperative hemothorax, whereas another underwent rethoracotomy for recurrent hemorrhage after initial surgical treatment of hemothorax.
CONCLUSIONS: Thoracic pathologies following solid-organ transplant comprise a heterogeneous group of conditions requiring individualized multidisciplinary management. Surgical and interventional procedures play a pivotal role in both establishing definitive diagnoses and providing effective treatment. Early recognition, careful patient selection, and pathology-specific management strategies may improve clinical outcomes in this complex and high-risk population.
journal: Experimental and clinical transplantation : official journal of the Middle East Society for Organ Transplantation

title: Self-Fueling Nanobacteria Harnesses Leaked Pancreatic Fluid to Eradicate Residual Tumors After Surgery.
abstract: Postoperative management of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains hindered by two closely linked challenges: the harmful effects of pancreatic fistula and the high risk of local tumor recurrence. Although leaked pancreatic fluid (PF) is generally regarded as a postoperative complication, its abundance of digestive enzymes also suggests an underexplored therapeutic opportunity. Here, we developed a localized therapeutic strategy that converts the enzyme-rich fistula microenvironment from a pathological burden into an antitumor resource. To achieve this, we nano-engineered Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron (B.t.) and integrated it with TRPV1 antagonist-loaded nanomicelles in a GelMA hydrogel, generating the platform TNPs-N@B.t. + Gel. Mechanistically, this system acts in a coordinated manner within the postoperative PDAC microenvironment. B.t. degrades tumor-associated mucins, thereby dismantling the protective barrier that shields PDAC cells from pancreatic enzymes and restoring their vulnerability to enzymatic attack. Meanwhile, PF forms an in situ digestive enzyme corona on the nanoengineered bacterial surface, which promotes deeper tumor penetration by disrupting intercellular adhesion. In parallel, delivery of the TRPV1 antagonist (TRPV1a) suppresses CGRP release, attenuates cancer-associated fibroblast (CAF) activation, and facilitates NK-cell-associated antitumor responses. In postoperative PDAC models, TNPs-N@B.t. + Gel showed durable local retention, enhanced tumor accumulation, suppressed recurrence, prolonged survival, and alleviated pain-related behaviors without evident systemic toxicity.

title: Skeletal Muscle Index, Tumor and Systemic Immunity, and Survival in Advanced Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: This study investigated relationships between the skeletal muscle index (SMI) and the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME), peripheral immune phenotypes, and serum biomarkers in advanced pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) and evaluated the prognostic significance of these parameters.
METHODS: A retrospective analysis of 119 advanced PDAC patients was performed. Sarcopenia was diagnosed using sex-specific SMI cut-offs from baseline L3-level computed tomography (CT) images. The TIME was characterized by multiplex immunofluorescence (mIF; n = 31), peripheral immunity by flow cytometry, and serum biomarkers by routine testing. Associations with SMI were examined using Spearman correlation; prognostic relevance was assessed using Cox proportional hazards models.
RESULTS: Sarcopenia (56/119, 47.1%) was associated with shorter progression-free survival (PFS) (8.83 vs. 12.03 months, p = 0.016) and overall survival (OS) (10.20 vs. 17.33 months, p = 0.014). SMI correlated most strongly with stromal CD8+ T cells (ρ = 0.52), stromal total T cells (ρ = 0.52), and stromal M2 macrophages (ρ = 0.50) in the TIME; with circulating Th2-like cells (ρ = -0.58) and CD4+ memory T cells (ρ = 0.45) peripherally; and with hemoglobin (ρ = 0.32) among serum markers. In multivariable Cox regression, stromal CD4+ Treg percentage independently predicted OS (hazard ratio [HR] = 7.60, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.60-36.22, p = 0.011), stromal CD56dim natural killer (NK)-cell density predicted PFS (HR = 1.015, 95% CI 1.001-1.028, p = 0.031), and the lymphocyte-to-monocyte ratio (LMR) predicted both PFS (HR = 0.86, p = 0.023) and OS (HR = 0.83, p = 0.009). No peripheral lymphocyte subset reached prognostic significance.
CONCLUSION: SMI is broadly associated with local and systemic immune phenotypes in advanced PDAC. Stromal CD4+ regulatory T cells (Tregs), CD56dim NK cells, and LMR carry independent prognostic information and may complement body-composition assessment.

title: Bismuth-Triggered Copper Release From CuS Nanosheets Enables Synergistic Ion-Interference and Chemodynamic/Photothermal Therapy.
abstract: Despite the promising potential of Cu-based nanozymes in cancer therapy, the therapeutic efficacy remains limited by the difficulty of achieving controlled Cu-ion release without compromising lattice integrity and catalytic activity. Herein, we developed a therapeutic nanoplatform utilizing bismuth (Bi)-doping techniques to control the release of copper (Cu) ions, enabling synergistic ion interference therapy, chemodynamic therapy (CDT) and photothermal therapy (PTT) for tumor treatment. Based on the instability of Bi-based compounds in the tumor microenvironment (TME), Bi ions are preferentially released from Bi-doped CuS nanosheets (Bi-CuS NSs), exposing more Cu vacancies and facilitating Cu ion release compared to CuS NSs. More importantly, upon cellular internalization, the released copper ions induce ionic homeostasis disruption, leading to cuproptosis in liver cancer cells. Simultaneously, the Cu vacancies generated by ion release enhance the peroxidase-like activity to produce more reactive oxygen species and improve the photothermal conversion efficiency to induce localized hyperthermia, synergistically amplifying tumor cell destruction. Consequently, Bi-CuS NSs exhibit excellent potential for synergistic metal ion interference and photothermal/chemodynamic therapy, enabling the multimodal treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma. This study presents a Bi-mediated strategy for regulating Cu-ion release and catalytic activity in metal-based cancer nanomedicines.

title: [Corrigendum] Acquired resistance of pancreatic cancer cells to treatment with gemcitabine and HER‑inhibitors is accompanied by increased sensitivity to STAT3 inhibition.
abstract: Following the publication of the above article, an interested reader drew the authors' attention to the fact that, for the western blots shown in Fig. 5 on p. 914, the β‑actin blots shown in the rightmost lanes for the 'BcPc3 OSIR' blots (the 'Crixotinib' and 'Af+Cr' lanes of the gel) were strikingly similar to the β‑actin blots shown in Fig. 2B (for the 'BxPc3 parental' blots), albeit with horizontal and vertical resizing of the bands concerned. Upon contacting the authors, they realized that Fig. 5 had inadvertently been assembled incorrectly (the same β‑actin cropped image was used for both samples in question after the files had erroneously being saved under the same name). The authors were able to consult their original data, and provided the Editorial Office with access to the images of the relevant full‑length original blots. The revised version of Fig. 5, now showing the correct data for the β‑actin blots for the 'BcPc3 OSIR' experiments, is shown on the next page. Note that this error did not affect the overall conclusions reported in the study. The authors are grateful to the Editor of International Journal of Oncology for allowing them this opportunity to publish a Corrigendum, and all the authors agree with its publication. Furthermore, the authors thank the interested reader for drawing this error in their paper to their attention, and apologize to the readership for any inconvenience caused. [International Journal of Oncology 48: 908‑918, 2016; DOI: 10.3892/ijo.2016.3320].

title: Gut Microbiota and Nutritional Aspects in Pancreatic Diseases: A Narrative Review.
abstract: Pancreatic diseases, including acute pancreatitis (AP) and chronic pancreatitis (CP), pancreatogenic diabetes mellitus (T3cDM), autoimmune pancreatitis (AIP), and pancreatic cancer (PDAC), are associated with metabolic, inflammatory, and nutritional disturbances. Increasing evidence indicates a bidirectional relationship between pancreatic diseases and the gut microbiota. On the one hand, alterations in microbial composition and function, intestinal barrier dysfunction, and bacterial translocation may contribute to their pathogenesis and progression. On the other hand, pancreatic diseases and associated changes in nutrition and treatment may affect the composition and function of the gut microbiota. This narrative review aimed to discuss the role of the gut microbiota and nutritional aspects in selected pancreatic diseases. PubMed/MEDLINE was searched up to May 2026 for English-language publications, with emphasis on studies from the previous 10 years, while earlier relevant studies were also considered. Google Scholar was used as a supplementary source. Human observational, experimental and mechanistic studies, as well as secondary literature, were considered, addressing pancreatic microbiota, intestinal permeability, bacterial translocation, nutrition, and microbiota-targeted interventions. Available evidence indicates that pancreatic diseases are associated with alterations in gut and pancreatic microbial communities, although the reported patterns vary between diseases and studies. These changes may be relevant to intestinal barrier integrity, inflammatory signaling, microbial metabolite production, and, in pancreatic cancer, the tumor microenvironment and treatment response. Nutritional management remains an important component of care, particularly in patients with exocrine pancreatic insufficiency and those at risk of malnutrition. However, the causal relationships between pancreatic diseases and microbiota alterations remain incompletely established, and evidence for microbiota-targeted interventions is limited and heterogeneous. Further clinical studies are needed to clarify these interactions and their potential diagnostic and therapeutic relevance.

title: Prehabilitation as a Strategy to Modulate the Tumor Microenvironment in Pancreatic Cancer.
abstract: Multimodal prehabilitation aims to enhance resilience to cancer therapy through exercise, nutrition, and psychological optimization. While prehabilitation can improve physical condition and functional status, its biologic influence on the tumor microenvironment (TME) remains poorly characterized. In pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), the TME is dominated by immunosuppressive and desmoplastic features that limit immune cell infiltration and therapeutic efficacy. As an exploratory pilot analysis, this study characterized the cellular composition, spatial relationships, and functional signaling of the pancreatic TME in patients who underwent prehabilitation prior to surgical resection and those who did not. Tumor samples from eight patients (four prehabilitation, four control) were analyzed with a 34-plex protein panel using Imaging Mass Cytometry (IMC), categorizing the tumor-immune landscape and functional status at the single-cell resolution. Prehabilitation tumors demonstrated reduced neutrophil and epithelial/tumor cell density and enrichment of Natural Killer (NK), CD4+, and CD8+ T cells. Spatial analysis revealed an immune-permissive architecture in prehabilitation tumors, in contrast to immune-resistant patterns in controls. Functional marker analysis showed reduced activation and pro-tumor signaling in immunosuppressive populations, including Tregs (HLADR, pAkt, pNFκB) and Collagen+ CAFs (NOS2, pERK, pNFκB, pSTAT3). These preliminary findings raise the possibility that prehabilitation is associated with an immune-permissive TME in PDAC, supporting further investigation of its immunomodulatory potential in larger, prospectively designed cohorts.

title: p38α Signaling Is Associated with Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma Progression and Represents a Potential Therapeutic Vulnerability.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is one of the most lethal malignancies, and approximately 15% of cases arise from intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms (IPMNs). These precursor lesions can progress to invasive cancer through the accumulation of molecular alterations. To identify pathways associated with this transition, we performed comparative transcriptomic analyses of patient-derived IPMN and PDAC samples, followed by protein-level validation in tissue specimens and pancreatic cancer cell lines. Functional studies were conducted using the selective p38α inhibitor ralimetinib in two-dimensional cultures, three-dimensional tumorspheres, and patient-derived tumor organoids (PDTOs). Transcriptomic profiling revealed significant downregulation of the p38 pathway in IPMNs compared with PDAC, suggesting progressive pathway activation during pancreatic tumorigenesis. Immunohistochemical analyses confirmed increased phospho-activated p38α in PDAC tissues, particularly in lesions with advanced malignant features, while PDAC cell lines displayed higher levels of activated p38α than non-tumorigenic pancreatic epithelial cells. Pharmacological inhibition of p38α suppressed downstream MAPKAPK2 phosphorylation, induced apoptotic cell death, and reduced tumorsphere growth and viability. Consistently, PDTOs exhibiting elevated p38α activation showed increased sensitivity to ralimetinib treatment. Collectively, these findings identify p38α signaling as a pathway activated during PDAC progression and support further investigation of p38α-targeted therapies as a potential precision medicine strategy for pancreatic cancer.

title: MYC-SNHG7-miR-34a-5p Feedback Loop Orchestrates GSDMD-Dependent Pyroptosis in Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
abstract: Pyroptosis is an immunogenic form of regulated cell death mediated by NLRP3 inflammasome activation, caspase-1, and gasdermin D. Unlike apoptosis, pyroptosis promotes anti-tumor immunity through IL-1β and IL-18 release, making it a promising therapeutic target in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Although the SNHG7/miR-34a/SIRT1 axis has been experimentally linked to NLRP3-dependent pyroptosis, whether it functions as a systems-level regulatory module coordinating the balance between drug resistance and multiple cell-fate outcomes remains unknown. To address this question, we developed a network medicine framework using a Boolean network model integrating drug resistance, senescence, apoptosis, and pyroptosis pathways in HCC. The model was constructed from experimentally validated molecular interactions and independently validated using gain- and loss-of-function perturbation studies that were not used during model construction, demonstrating strong agreement with experimental observations. Our analysis identified a previously unreported MYC-SNHG7-miR-34a double-negative feedback loop, establishing miR-34a as a central regulatory hub controlling cell-fate decisions. Perturbation analysis predicted that SNHG7 inhibition shifts cells from drug resistance toward pyroptosis, identifying restoration of miR-34a activity as a potential strategy to induce immunogenic cell death. These findings provide a systems-level framework for therapeutic targeting of the MYC-SNHG7-miR-34a axis in HCC.

title: Rewiring Biological Barriers in Pancreatic Diseases with Metal-Organic Frameworks.
abstract: Pancreatic diseases, particularly pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), remain among the most challenging disorders to diagnose and treat owing to a series of interconnected biological barriers, including dense stromal desmoplasia, profound immunosuppression, hypoxia, therapeutic resistance, and the lack of effective early-detection strategies. Overcoming these barriers requires multifunctional platforms capable of integrating diagnosis, microenvironment regulation, and precision therapy within a single system. Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), a class of highly tunable porous crystalline materials, have emerged as uniquely suited candidates for this purpose because of their programmable composition, structural versatility, catalytic activity, and capacity for multifunctional integration. Notably, MOFs have evolved from passive drug carriers into active regulators of disease-associated biological processes, enabling enhanced drug delivery, extracellular matrix remodeling, ferroptosis- and cuproptosis-based precision therapy, energy-triggered reactive oxygen species generation, immune microenvironment reprogramming, and imaging-guided theranostics. Beyond pancreatic cancer, emerging evidence further supports their potential applications in pancreatitis management and interventional therapeutic enhancement. In this review, we systematically summarize recent advances in the rational engineering of MOFs for pancreatic diseases, focusing on how material design strategies are leveraged to overcome key pathological barriers and improve therapeutic outcomes. We further discuss current challenges associated with biosafety, biodegradation, large-scale manufacturing, and clinical translation, while highlighting future opportunities for the development of next-generation MOF-based precision nanomedicines. By integrating advances across materials science, nanomedicine, and pancreatic disease biology, this review provides a comprehensive framework for the design and translational development of MOF-enabled diagnostic and therapeutic platforms.

title: Corosolic Acid in Hepatocellular Carcinoma: Molecular Properties, Evidence Boundaries, and Development Priorities.
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common primary liver cancer and remains a major cause of cancer-related death worldwide. Corosolic acid (CA), an ursane-type pentacyclic triterpenoid with antidiabetic, anti-inflammatory, and antitumour activities, has attracted interest as a potential natural compound for HCC treatment. This review critically evaluates CA as a molecular lead for HCC by integrating its physicochemical characteristics with direct preclinical evidence, cross-model hypotheses, and development constraints. Current studies indicate that CA suppresses HCC cell proliferation and migration, disrupts cell-cycle progression, and promotes cell death, with antitumour effects also observed in animal models. These activities have been associated with mitochondrial apoptosis and endoplasmic reticulum stress, Yes-associated protein (YAP)-related growth regulation, increased susceptibility to ferroptosis, and inhibition of vascular endothelial growth factor receptor 2 (VEGFR2)-related migratory signalling. Interestingly, evidence from other tumour, metabolic, inflammatory, and fibrotic models further suggests that CA may influence tumour metabolism, autophagy, the immunosuppressive microenvironment, fibrosis, and angiogenesis. However, these cross-model findings require direct validation in HCC. Although CA shows promising preclinical activity, it should be regarded as a natural lead compound rather than an established HCC therapy. Major unresolved gaps include poorly defined dose-exposure-response relationships, limited validation of the principal mechanisms in clinically relevant HCC models, and insufficient evidence that optimised formulations or combination regimens improve efficacy without increasing toxicity.

title: Targeting SERPINB5 and MSLN for Pancreatic Cancer Therapy.
abstract: Background/Objectives: Pancreatic cancer (PC) is a leading cause of cancer-related death in the United States and lacks efficient therapeutic options. Serine peptidase inhibitor, clade B, member 5 (SERPINB5) is non-inhibitory toward serine proteases, yet it has diverse biological functions, including regulating cell migration, cell death, gene expression, and stress responses. Mesothelin (MSLN) is a tumor-associated antigen that is broadly overexpressed on various malignant tumor cells and plays a crucial role in promoting proliferation, invasion, and metastasis. Methods: We integrated public database analyses, cell-line screening, gene knockdown and overexpression, immunoblotting, cell viability and apoptosis assays, flow cytometry, chromatin immunoprecipitation paired with quantitative PCR (ChIP-qPCR), and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy to investigate SERPINB5 and MSLN functions, developing a novel and effective therapeutic strategy for patients with pancreatic cancer. Results: Both SERPINB5 and MSLN are highly expressed and negatively associated with the overall survival of PC patients. Our mechanistic study suggests that SERPINB5 negatively regulates the mitochondrial protein dehydrogenase/reductase 2 (DHRS2) to promote PC cell survival; consequently, SERPINB5 depletion induces PC cell apoptosis. Of note, SERPINB5 depletion increases MSLN transcription by enhancing c-Myc binding to the MSLN promoter region, which in turn suppresses the mitochondrial protein DHRS2 and leads to resistance to apoptosis in PC cells. Our genetic ablation study shows that SERPINB5 and MSLN are critical for PC cell survival, and that depleting both proteins synergistically induces PC cell apoptosis. Gemcitabine (GEM) is a standard chemotherapy drug for PC treatment. Our study shows that SERPINB5-high PC cells display greater sensitivity to GEM than SERPINB5-low PC cells. GEM treatment increases mitochondrial DHRS2 protein expression, similar to the effect of SERPINB5 knockdown, whereas upregulated MSLN confers apoptotic resistance by decreasing DHRS2 levels. Conclusions: Our in vitro study demonstrates that sequential treatment with GEM followed by anti-MSLN chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cells is an effective and promising strategy for patients with pancreatic cancer. Future studies using mouse models may validate the efficacy of this sequential treatment strategy in vivo.

title: SPINT2 Is Associated with Dual-Phenotype Hepatocellular Carcinoma and Aggressive Tumor Features.
abstract: Background: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) heterogeneity, particularly the presence of tumor cells co-expressing hepatocytic and cholangiocytic markers, contributes to therapeutic resistance and poor prognosis, yet its molecular correlates remain incompletely understood. This study aimed to characterize dual-phenotype HCC (DPHCC) and investigate the association and functional relevance of SPINT2 in tumor progression. Methods: We integrated multiplex immunofluorescence, CyTOF mass cytometry, single-cell RNA sequencing, and functional assays across clinical cohorts and cell lines. Results: Multiplex staining identified DPHCC in 22.89% of patients, correlating significantly with younger age, elevated AFP, and inferior recurrence-free and overall survival compared to non-DPHCC cases. Parallel scRNA-seq and CyTOF analyses showed that DPHCC-associated cells were enriched for stemness- and EMT-related features, with SPINT2 emerging as a top candidate gene in the transcriptomic analysis. Immunohistochemistry showed higher SPINT2 expression in DPHCC tissues, and high SPINT2 expression was associated with shorter overall survival in univariate Kaplan-Meier analysis and frequently co-localized with CK19. Functionally, SPINT2 modulation produced context-dependent changes in invasion, proliferation-related CCK-8 readouts, wound closure, sphere formation, and xenograft tumor growth in MHCC-97H and MHCC-LM3 cells. Collectively, these findings characterize DPHCC as a clinically relevant dual-lineage phenotypic state associated with aggressive tumor features and identify SPINT2 as a candidate molecule associated with this phenotype. Conclusions: SPINT2 is associated with the DPHCC-related state and aggressive tumor-cell phenotypes, but its mechanistic and clinical significance requires further validation.

title: Tumour Mutation Burden Does Not Predict Immune Cell Frequency or Risk of Recurrence After Surgery in Hepatocellular Carcinoma.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION/OBJECTIVES: Understanding the genetic and immune heterogeneity in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is critical for accurate pathological characterisation and treatment planning, as therapies advance towards personalisation. Tumour mutational burden (TMB) has been proposed as a biomarker of response to immune checkpoint blockade but its relationship with immune infiltration in HCC remains unclear, particularly across different aetiologies and within multifocal disease.
METHODS: This study characterises both the inter- and intra-patient heterogeneity in HCC, integrating whole-exome sequencing with detailed histopathologic and immune cell profiling, to identify implications for diagnosis and response to treatment. Samples of 54 tumours from 26 patients undergoing surgery at the Leeds Teaching Hospital NHS Trust were examined, including 10 patients with multifocal disease. The cohort includes the major UK aetiological groups. Whole-exome sequencing of tumours and matched background liver identified somatic variants. Histopathological and immunohistochemical evaluations were performed to assess tumour features and characterise the tumour immune microenvironment.
RESULTS: Marked inter-individual heterogeneity was observed across aetiological groups with variation in tumour mutation burden, genes containing somatic mutations and immune infiltration. Multifocal tumours frequently demonstrated discordant genetic and immune profiles irrespective of clonal relatedness. NeoTMB was not associated with recurrence following surgery, whereas recurrent cases demonstrated significantly higher intratumoural FoxP3+ T-cell frequencies.
CONCLUSIONS: This study demonstrates substantial genetic and immune heterogeneity in HCC, including marked discordance between multifocal tumours within the same patient. Tumour mutation burden was not related to immune cell infiltration or risk of recurrence after surgery, whereas elevated intratumoural FoxP3+ regulatory T-cell frequencies were associated with recurrence. These findings suggest that the immunological composition of the tumour microenvironment may be more relevant to clinical outcome than mutational burden alone and highlight the importance of comprehensive tumour profiling to inform personalised therapeutic strategies.

title: Decoding the Cellular Response to Methylthioadenosine Uncovers Novel Targets for Chronic Liver Disease.
abstract: Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis type 3 (PFIC3), caused by MDR3 deficiency (MDR2 in mice), is a lethal pediatric liver disease characterized by early-onset persistent cholestasis, progressive fibrosis, cirrhosis, and eventual liver failure. MDR3 is a phosphatidylcholine transporter located in the canalicular membrane of hepatocytes, and its deficiency leads to the accumulation of free bile acids, which damage epithelial cells due to their detergent-like effect. Therapeutic options remain limited, highlighting the need to identify molecular drivers of disease progression and novel pharmacological strategies. To investigate the molecular alterations associated with this deficiency, our laboratory performed functional proteomic analyses in patient samples and murine hepatic organoids, revealing consistent reprogramming of one-carbon metabolism (OCM). Based on these findings, we explored the therapeutic potential and molecular mechanisms of 5'-methylthioadenosine (MTA), a metabolite involved in this pathway. Using hepatocellular carcinoma cells (PLCs), we combined quantitative shotgun proteomics with the proteome integral solubility alteration (PISA) assay to characterize functional responses and identify direct protein targets of MTA. To reinforce the physiological relevance of our findings, we extended the PISA analysis to liver protein extracts from the Mdr2-/- mouse model of chronic cholestatic injury, enabling validation of candidate target interactions observed in cellular extracts. Proteomic profiling revealed that MTA induces significant alterations in cell division processes, epigenetic regulatory networks, and energy metabolism, thereby promoting an adaptive phenotype characterized by metabolic plasticity, microenvironmental reorganization, and immunomodulation. These findings provide a robust molecular framework for understanding the hepatic response to MTA and shed new light on the mechanisms that may underlie its beneficial effects. In addition, they provide a valuable platform for further investigation of the therapeutic potential of this compound and its prospective translation into clinical practice.

title: Molecularly Guided Therapy and the Tumor Microenvironment in Advanced Cholangiocarcinoma: Current Evidence and Emerging Strategies Targeting FGFR2, HER2, and IDH1 with Pemigatinib, Zanidatamab, and Ivosidenib.
abstract: Cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) remains an aggressive malignancy characterized by late-stage diagnosis, substantial molecular heterogeneity, and limited therapeutic options. Advances in molecular characterization have identified actionable alterations and expanded systemic treatment beyond conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy. This review examines three clinically relevant and mechanistically distinct targeted strategies in advanced CCA. Pemigatinib, a selective fibroblast growth factor receptor 1-3 (FGFR1-3) inhibitor, targets oncogenic signaling driven by FGFR2 fusions or rearrangements, which occur predominantly in intrahepatic CCA. Zanidatamab, a bispecific human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-directed antibody targeting two extracellular HER2 domains, provides a therapeutic approach for HER2-positive biliary tract cancers (BTCs). Ivosidenib, a selective inhibitor of mutant isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 (IDH1m), suppresses production of the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate and targets the associated metabolic and epigenetic dysregulation in IDH1-mutant CCA. The review integrates the molecular rationale and pivotal clinical evidence supporting these therapies with their safety profiles, mechanisms of acquired resistance, biomarker selection, and therapeutic positioning. Particular attention is given to tumor heterogeneity and the tumor microenvironment as determinants of treatment response and resistance, as well as to emerging strategies involving next-generation inhibitors, antibody-drug conjugates, immunotherapy, rational combinations, and longitudinal molecular monitoring. Collectively, the clinical development of pemigatinib, zanidatamab, and ivosidenib demonstrates the therapeutic value of matching actionable molecular alterations with mechanism-based treatments, while highlighting the need to overcome resistance and optimize treatment sequencing to achieve more durable benefit in advanced CCA.

title: MAP2-mediated integrin dysregulation reprograms cancer cell plasticity in hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: Targeting tumor cell plasticity is central to overcome drug resistance and metastasis. Through lineage-tracing and lineage-ablation studies, our team has previously shown hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells marked by CD133 to represent a functional subset displaying dedifferentiated status with stemness traits, yet there are limited therapies effective for eradicating such resilient cell populations. Here, we explore the therapeutic potential of repurposing an existing drug estramustine phosphate (EMP) for targeting HCC plasticity through inhibiting MAP2, a gene uniquely enriched in CD133+ 'HCC' stemness subset but not in CD133+ 'normal' regenerative cells. MAP2 is transcriptionally activated by histone 3 lysine 27 acetylation and its upregulation correlates with aggressive clinical features. Mechanistically, MAP2 sustains tumor plasticity and transition to a mesenchymal state through inducing filamentous actin polymerization and YAP activation, which subsequently disrupts integrin expression and cell adhesions. Our research offers a promising opportunity for drug repurposing using EMP in combination with sorafenib to target HCC at its stemness roots.

title: Sequential Dual Nanoparticle Approach for Extracellular Matrix Remodeling and Targeted Chemotherapy through Liposome-Exosome Hybridization in Pancreatic Cancer.
abstract: Pancreatic cancer remains one of the most aggressive and treatment-resistant malignancies, with a poor prognosis and limited response to conventional therapies. Although liposomal doxorubicin (DOX) formulations reduce systemic toxicity, their clinical use is constrained by insufficient tumor targeting and poor intratumoral penetration. Here, we report a sequential dual-nanoparticle approach that integrates extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling with tumor-targeted chemotherapy to overcome these barriers. Hyaluronidase-loaded liposomes (LH) were first employed to degrade hyaluronic acid-rich ECM, followed by the administration of DOX-loaded liposome-exosome hybrid nanoparticles (HLD) engineered using pancreatic cancer cell-derived exosomes to confer intrinsic tumor-homing capability. The DOX-loaded hybrid nanoparticles demonstrated enhanced cellular uptake, potent cytotoxicity, and strong immunogenic cell death (ICD) responses in pancreatic cancer cells. ECM degradation by LH significantly improved intratumoral accumulation and penetration of subsequently administered HLD in vivo. In a pancreatic cancer xenograft model, sequential LH and HLD treatment resulted in superior tumor growth suppression compared with monotherapies, without inducing systemic toxicity. Collectively, this work demonstrates a modular, sequential nanotherapeutic platform that synergistically combines ECM remodeling and exosome-mediated targeting, offering a promising strategy to improve drug delivery and therapeutic efficacy in stromal-dense solid tumors, such as pancreatic cancer.

title: MRI-Only Preoperative Localization and Semiautomated Three-Dimensional Modeling of the Cervical Vagus Nerve for Vagus Nerve Stimulation Implantation.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: We evaluated whether three-dimensional steady-state free precession with time-spatial labeling inversion pulse (3D-SSFP with time-SLIP) MRI could localize the cervical vagus nerve before vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) implantation and developed training-data-free semiautomated vagus nerve tracking software.
METHODS: Thirty patients with drug-resistant epilepsy underwent preoperative cervical 3D-SSFP with time-SLIP MRI followed by VNS implantation. The left vagus nerve was visually identified at the planned surgical level, and its relationship to the common carotid artery (CCA) and internal jugular vein (IJV) was classified. MRI localization was validated against intraoperative findings. A MATLAB-based tool semi-automatically tracked the vagus nerve, CCA, and IJV from user-defined reference points. Accuracy was assessed using coordinate error and classification agreement.
RESULTS: The vagus nerve was identified on MRI in all 30 patients, with complete concordance between MRI and intraoperative localization. Among 29 classifiable patients, the nerve was located superficially between the CCA and IJV in 45%, superficially and lateral to the CCA in 41%, deep between the CCA and IJV in 10%, and deep and medial to the CCA in 3.4%. The median distance between software-derived and visually identified coordinates was 1 mm (interquartile range, 1-2 mm), and software-derived classification agreed with consensus visual classification in 27 of 29 patients (93%).
CONCLUSIONS: Cervical MRI enabled preoperative localization of the vagus nerve and adjacent vessels. The semiautomated method showed close agreement with expert visual assessment and may support anatomical orientation and surgical planning for VNS implantation.

title: NUPR1-positive tumor-associated macrophages facilitate the progression of hepatocellular carcinoma via ferroptosis resistance.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) are major contributors to the immunosuppressive microenvironment of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Nuclear protein 1 (NUPR1) is a stress-responsive regulator implicated in tumor progression; however, whether it functionally controls ferroptosis-associated stress adaptation in TAMs and thereby sustains their immunosuppressive phenotype remains unclear.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: Single-cell RNA sequencing and multiplex immunohistochemistry identified and validated NUPR1-expressing TAMs in human HCC. Pharmacological and genetic approaches assessed macrophage polarization, ferroptosis-associated changes, and tumor-supportive activity. Readouts included lipid peroxidation, Fe2+ accumulation, GPX4 expression and activity, redox homeostasis, and mitochondrial membrane potential. GPX4 rescue and pharmacological ferroptosis modulation evaluated the functional involvement of GPX4-associated ferroptosis resistance. Primary bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs) and an immunocompetent orthotopic HCC model provided additional validation.
RESULTS: NUPR1 was enriched in CD163+ TAMs within HCC tissues. In THP-1-derived macrophages, NUPR1 inhibition enhanced ferroptosis-associated changes and attenuated M2-like polarization and tumor-supportive functions, whereas NUPR1 overexpression produced the opposite effects. GPX4 overexpression partially rescued the ferroptosis-associated and macrophage phenotypic changes induced by NUPR1 silencing, whereas RSL3 attenuated the effects of NUPR1 overexpression. Primary BMDMs supported the macrophage phenotypic findings. In the orthotopic model, NUPR1 inhibition suppressed tumor growth and was accompanied by altered macrophage-associated markers and enhanced ferroptosis-associated changes.
CONCLUSION: NUPR1 promotes HCC progression, at least in part, by modulating GPX4-associated ferroptosis-related stress and sustaining the M2-like immunosuppressive phenotype of TAMs.

title: Antibody-drug conjugates as promising platform for intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma: molecular insights, drug-delivery challenges, and emerging therapeutic targets.
abstract: Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA) is the second most prevalent primary hepatic malignancy with increasing incidence, poor prognosis, recurrence, and limited therapies. Currently, surgical resection remains the only potentially curative treatment for iCCA. The main challenge, even after surgery, is that small or poorly cellular liver tumors may recur a year later if minimal residual disease goes undetected. Additionally, the majority of chemotherapy and targeted therapies have modest clinical benefit due to tumor heterogeneity and therapeutic resistance. Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) have recently emerged as a promising targeted therapeutic platform by combining the tumor specificity of monoclonal antibodies with highly potent cytotoxic payloads, thereby enabling selective drug delivery while minimizing systemic toxicity. This review comprehensively summarizes the molecular landscape of iCCA relevant to ADC development and discusses clinically significant targets, including HER2, FGFR2, TROP2, Claudin-1, MUC1, EpCAM, and EGFR. The structural and functional significance of ADC components, including antibodies, linkers, and payloads, are also discussed in relation to therapeutic efficacy and safety. Furthermore, current preclinical and clinical progress involving ADC-based therapies for iCCA and related cholangiocarcinoma is highlighted. Tumor heterogenicity, drug resistance, desmoplastic tumor microenvironment, and low antigen binding are among the primary barriers to the development of ADCs for iCCA that are critically discussed. Additionally, the prospects for the next generation, including bispecific ADCs and dual-payload conjugates for iCCA, were explored. Collectively, ADCs represent a rapidly evolving precision oncology platform with considerable potential to improve therapeutic outcomes and future management strategies for patients with iCCA.

title: Hippo signaling drives mesenchymal cell fate and heterogeneity in liver cancer.
abstract:
BACKGROUND & AIMS: Liver cancer comprises a spectrum of cancers that include pure hepatocellular carcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma, and tumors with varying degrees of mixed hepatocytic, cholangiocytic, and mesenchymal traits. Such heterogeneity can elevate cancer aggressiveness and induce therapy resistance. However, mechanisms that promote cellular plasticity in cancer remain poorly understood. To study mechanisms driving heterogeneity in liver cancer, we developed a mouse model in which cholangiocarcinoma cells spontaneously acquire mesenchymal characteristics.
METHODS: We induced liver cancer in mice by hydrodynamic tail vein injection of plasmids expressing activated versions of Notch, Akt, and KRas. We performed lineage tracing, single nucleus RNA-sequencing, and gain- and loss-of-function experiments of Hippo signaling to determine the mechanisms inducing tumor heterogeneity.
RESULTS: Co-expression of activated Notch, Akt, and KRas led to the formation of aggressive intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (ICC) that presented a strong desmoplastic reaction and a heterogeneous population of cancer cells with varying levels of epithelial and mesenchymal features. Single-cell analysis showed that these tumors comprised cancer cells with cholangiocyte-like epithelial (N = 4006 cells) and mesenchymal (N = 605 cells) characters. Lineage tracing revealed that the mesenchymal cancer cells originated from the transdifferentiation of epithelial cancer cells. Mechanistically, we identified the Hippo pathway effectors Yap and Taz as drivers of this transition: high Yap/Taz levels correlated with the acquisition of mesenchymal features, Yap/Taz double mutant tumor cells were unable to transdifferentiate into mesenchymal tumor cells (N = 5, p = 0.007), and overexpression of Yap (N = 5, p = 0.008) or Taz (N = 5, p = 0.025) in pure ICC tumors driven by Notch and Akt led to the emergence of cancer cells with mesenchymal features.
CONCLUSIONS: Our data show that the Hippo pathway effectors Yap and Taz drive plasticity in liver cancer cells and promote the transdifferentiation of epithelial cholangiocarcinoma cells into tumor cells with mesenchymal characteristics.
IMPACT AND IMPLICATIONS: Our study provides a mechanistic understanding of how cellular heterogeneity, a major challenge for treatment, develops in intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma. We show that the Hippo pathway effectors Yap and Taz drive the transition of epithelial liver cancer cells into a mesenchymal state. These findings are important because they identify molecular mechanisms that promote cholangiocarcinoma plasticity and imply that therapeutic targeting of YAP/TAZ activity may inhibit cancer cell plasticity and enhance treatment efficacy in patients with cholangiocarcinoma and other cancers with similar molecular features. However, given the complexity of tumor signaling and the preclinical nature of our mouse model, additional validation is needed to define its clinical relevance.

title: Transcriptomic analysis reveals AURKB promotes malignant progression of hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: Due to the poor prognosis of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), there is an urgent need to identify novel therapeutic targets. This study aims to evaluate the potential of Aurora kinase B (AURKB) as a therapeutic target for HCC and provide a theoretical basis for immunotherapy in HCC. In this study, 374 patients were included from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database, and single-sample gene set enrichment analysis was performed to classify them into high-immunity and low-immunity groups. Through differential gene expression analysis and univariate Cox regression analysis, AURKB was screened out as a risk gene, followed by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis, immune infiltration analysis, and pathway enrichment analysis. The results demonstrated that overexpression of AURKB was associated with worse overall survival (OS) and disease-free survival (DFS) in HCC patients. High AURKB expression was correlated with increased infiltration of CD8 + T cells, macrophages, and dendritic cells, along with elevated expression of immune checkpoint molecules, including programmed death-1 (PD-1), cytotoxic T lymphocyte-associated antigen-4 (CTLA-4), CD80, and CD86. To further validate the role of AURKB in HCC, we constructed HCC cell lines with AURKB knockdown. Knockdown of AURKB inhibited HCC cell proliferation, colony formation, migration, and invasion. Functional experiments further indicate that AURKB promotes CD8 + T cell exhaustion and immune evasion. In conclusion, our study indicates that AURKB is an immune-related prognostic biomarker that promotes immune escape and tumor progression in HCC.

title: integrating single-cell transcriptomics and chromatin accessibility profiling to decipher the molecular landscape of Hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is a prevalent and lethal liver malignancy, characterized by high recurrence rates and limited therapeutic options. Current diagnostic and treatment strategies are hindered by drug resistance and a lack of effective biomarkers for early detection.
METHODS: This study aims to elucidate the role of lactylation and fibroblast cells within the tumor microenvironment (TME) of HCC, focusing on their potential as therapeutic targets. Utilizing a comprehensive multi-omics approach, we integrated single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and single-cell ATAC sequencing (scATAC-seq) data from public databases (GEO, TCGA) to explore transcriptional and epigenetic landscapes at single-cell resolution.
RESULTS: Our analysis identified fibroblast cells as key players with high lactylation-related pathway activity, and CREB1 as a central transcription factor regulating lactylation-associated genes in these cells. The CREB1 regulatory network was associated with specific immune cell infiltration patterns, drug sensitivity profiles, and enrichment in critical signaling pathways such as Chemokine, TNF, NF-κB, and EMT. These findings underscore the pivotal role of lactylation-driven epigenetic regulation in fibroblasts, influencing the HCC immune microenvironment and disease progression.

title: Decoding cellular vulnerabilities for interpretable drug response prediction.
abstract: Accurate prediction of anticancer drug response remains challenging because conventional approaches based on chemical structures and baseline molecular profiles do not directly capture drug-induced perturbations or cellular dependencies. Here, we present vulnerability-guided cascaded attention transformer (VCAT), which integrates Connectivity Map (CMap)/Library of Integrated Network-based Cellular Signatures (LINCS)-derived consensus transcriptional signatures with clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-supervised cellular representations through adaptive encoders and dual stream cascaded attention. Across four data splitting strategies, VCAT outperformed conventional machine learning and published deep learning models, achieving the best performance in 11 of 12 classification split metric comparisons. Ablation analyses showed that CRISPR-derived vulnerability features complement baseline gene expression and that the proposed interaction architecture further improves prediction. VCAT also enhanced continuous IC50 prediction and generalized across Cancer Therapeutics Response Portal (CTRP), Profiling Relative Inhibition Simultaneously in Mixtures (PRISM), patient-derived organoids, and hepatocellular carcinoma cohorts. Attention based prioritization and integrated gradients jointly highlighted biologically relevant genes, while knockdown of cytosolic iron-sulfur assembly component 3 (CIAO3), methylenetetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase 2 (MTHFD2), and WD repeat domain 1 (WDR1) increased sorafenib sensitivity in hepatocellular carcinoma cell lines. These findings support integrating drug-induced perturbations with genetic vulnerabilities for accurate, interpretable, and transferable anticancer drug response prediction.

title: BHLHE40 as a transcriptional rheostat: decoding microenvironmental signals in context-dependent tumor plasticity.
abstract: The basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor BHLHE40 (also known as BHLHB2, DEC1, STRA13) functions as a critical molecular rheostat in cancer biology, exhibiting context-dependent roles that contribute to tumor plasticity. This review synthesizes current knowledge of BHLHE40, with emphasis on its structural features, including DNA binding, dimerization, and regulatory domains, as well as its integration of key physiological signals, such as circadian rhythm regulation, hypoxic adaptation, cellular senescence, and immune modulation. Pancancer analyses indicate that BHLHE40 expression is dysregulated across multiple tumor types. Elevated expression is associated with poor prognosis in cancers such as glioblastoma, acute myeloid leukemia, and ovarian cancer, whereas it correlates with favorable outcomes in breast and kidney cancers. Notably, the functional role of BHLHE40 is highly tissue-dependent. It promotes tumor progression in hepatocellular carcinoma, gastric cancer, colorectal cancer, and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma by enhancing proliferation, invasion, migration, epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), and therapeutic resistance. In contrast, BHLHE40 exhibits tumor-suppressive effects in prostate cancer by inducing cellular senescence, and in endometrial cancer by inhibiting EMT. The tumor microenvironment plays a pivotal role in modulating BHLHE40 activity, with factors such as hypoxia, cytokine signaling, and immune cell interactions shaping its oncogenic or tumor-suppressive functions. Importantly, its role in maintaining CD8+ T-cell effector function during immune checkpoint blockade highlights its therapeutic potential. However, the context-dependent duality of BHLHE40 presents significant challenges for clinical targeting. Emerging therapeutic strategies, including targeted protein degradation approaches and advanced tumor models such as patient-derived organoids, offer promising avenues for intervention. Future studies integrating multi-omics data and spatial transcriptomics will be essential to fully elucidate the role of BHLHE40 and to harness its potential as a biomarker and therapeutic target for overcoming tumor progression, therapeutic resistance, and immune evasion.

title: Graph attention network-driven single-cell omics analysis reveals how B4GALNT1-mediated glycosylation remodelling of the ferroptosis-pyroptosis network promotes drug resistance in hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Acquired resistance to sorafenib in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is accompanied by coordinated changes in oxidative-stress handling and regulated cell-death pathways, yet how membrane organisation connects these adaptations is not fully resolved. We therefore examined whether B4GALNT1, a ganglioside biosynthetic glycosyltransferase, couples changes in ganglioside composition and lipid-raft architecture to ferroptosis regulation and caspase-1/GSDMD-associated signalling in sorafenib-resistant HCC.
METHODS: We combined TCGA-LIHC analysis, single-cell transcriptomics, pathway-level analyses, and graph attention network modelling with a treatment-annotated local cohort of 92 patients with HCC who received sorafenib. Functional experiments were conducted in Huh7/Huh7-SR cells and additional liver-tumour models using B4GALNT1 gain- and loss-of-function, an independent second-sgRNA knockout clone, GM1 rescue, and re-expression of either wild-type B4GALNT1 or the catalytic-loss D358A variant. Validation included ganglioside profiling, detergent-resistant membrane isolation, lipid-raft disruption/repletion, ferroptosis-directed pharmacology, cell-death measurements, and xenograft studies.
RESULTS: B4GALNT1 was enriched in tumour-associated hepatocyte populations and was upregulated in Huh7-SR cells. In the local cohort, higher B4GALNT1 protein abundance tracked with less favourable response to sorafenib and poorer survival outcomes. Increasing B4GALNT1 shifted ganglioside abundance toward GM2/GM1/GD2 and increased GM1-enriched raft-associated fractions, whereas knockout produced reciprocal changes. B4GALNT1-high cells showed increased GPX4 and SLC7A11, reduced lipid peroxidation and labile Fe2 +, and lower ferroptotic injury. At the same time, caspase-1/GSDMD-associated signalling and IL-1β/IL-18 release increased without widespread terminal membrane lysis. Exogenous GM1 partially rescued knockout-associated changes, and wild-type B4GALNT1 restored the phenotype more effectively than the D358A mutant. Concordant directional effects were observed in additional cell models and in xenografts.
CONCLUSIONS: The data are consistent with a model in which B4GALNT1 reshapes ganglioside composition and GM1-enriched membrane microdomains, thereby supporting a drug-adapted state that combines greater ferroptosis resistance with restricted caspase-1/GSDMD-associated membrane permeabilisation. This integrated phenotype accompanies reduced sorafenib responsiveness and offers a mechanistic basis for acquired resistance in HCC.
HIGHLIGHTS: B4GALNT1 is associated with sorafenib resistance and poorer outcomes in treated HCC. B4GALNT1 remodels gangliosides and lipid rafts, limiting ferroptotic injury. Caspase-1/GSDMD signalling increases without widespread terminal membrane lysis. Genetic rescue and cross-model studies support B4GALNT1 specificity.

title: Emphysematous Gastritis Precipitated by Malignant Gastric Outlet Obstruction from Advanced Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Emphysematous gastritis is a rare, frequently fatal infection of the gastric wall caused by gas-forming organisms. Gastric outlet obstruction is well recognised as a cause of benign gastric emphysema but is seldom reported as a precipitant of emphysematous gastritis. This report adds a rare presentation of emphysematous gastritis with malignant gastric outlet obstruction as a risk factor.
CASE DESCRIPTION: An 86-year-old man with locally advanced pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma presented after a fall preceded by generalised weakness, abdominal bloating, diarrhoea, nausea and fever. He was hypotensive and tachycardic, with acute kidney injury and severe high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Computed tomography scan demonstrated a markedly distended stomach with intramural gas and distal obstruction from progressive pancreatic malignancy; blood cultures were negative. He was managed non-operatively with aggressive resuscitation, broad-spectrum intravenous antibiotics and gastric decompression, with subsequent clinical, biochemical and radiological improvement.
CONCLUSION: Malignant gastric outlet obstruction, compounded by chemotherapy-related immunosuppression, can precipitate emphysematous gastritis. In selected patients without perforation or ischaemia, even those who are frail and immunocompromised, conservative management can achieve resolution.
LEARNING POINTS: Malignant gastric outlet obstruction from advanced pancreatic cancer can precipitate emphysematous gastritis, a rare and often fatal infection, particularly when compounded by chemotherapy-related immunosuppression.This case adds to the growing evidence that carefully selected patients without perforation or ischaemia can be managed conservatively with antibiotics and gastric decompression rather than surgery.
journal: European journal of case reports in internal medicine

title: Innate immunity-stroma crosstalk in pancreatic cancer: overcoming spatial and metabolic barriers to immunotherapy.
abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) exhibits profound resistance to current immunotherapies, a challenge largely attributed to its uniquely immunosuppressive and desmoplastic tumor microenvironment (TME). At the heart of this therapeutic recalcitrance lies the dynamic, bidirectional crosstalk between innate immune cells-particularly tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) and tumor-associated neutrophils (TANs)-and stromal components, notably cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs). This review comprehensively delineates how the innate immunity-stroma axis establishes formidable spatial and metabolic barriers that thwart effective antitumor immunity. Spatially, dense collagen matrices, periductal fibroblast organization, and neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) create physical checkpoints that exclude cytotoxic CD8+ T cells and natural killer (NK) cells from tumor nests. Metabolically, elevated lactate, cholesterol dysregulation, adenosine accumulation, and altered polyamine metabolism synergistically paralyze effector lymphocytes while driving immunosuppressive myeloid polarization. We highlight the key molecular networks orchestrating this pathological crosstalk, including the NF-κB, IL-1β, JAK/STAT3, and TGF-β signaling pathways. Furthermore, we summarize emerging therapeutic strategies designed to dismantle these barriers, encompassing macrophage reprogramming, CAF modulation, and metabolic interventions. Finally, we discuss the multidimensional "3D+R" framework-integrating de-desmoplasia, de-adenosine, de-novo antigen presentation, and rational sequencing-as a conceptual roadmap for rationally designed combination therapies to overcome PDAC immunotherapy resistance.

title: Basal Marker ΔNp63α Is Enriched in Pancreatic Cancer Metastases but Not in Primary Tumors Post-Chemotherapy.
abstract: Cancer cells within a single pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) are most often heterogeneous in their expression of the basal or classical transcriptional program. Predominance of the basal subtype has been associated with poorer patient outcomes and increased resistance to chemotherapy. Based on this, we predicted that basal subtype would be enriched in tumors previously treated with chemotherapy, and in metastases derived from primary PDAC tumors with a mixed basal/classical population. To create matched classical and basal cell lines, we stably transduced two classical PDAC cell lines (AsPC1 and HPAFII) with the basal program transcriptional driver ∆Np63α or an mCherry control and assessed their growth, metastasis, and response to chemotherapy both in vitro and in vivo. Forced expression of ∆Np63α successfully converted both cell lines to basal transcriptomic subtype, yet the basal program failed to drive increased cell growth or chemoresistance in culture and did not affect tumor growth of AsPC1 in the murine pancreas. In mice orthotopically engrafted with ∆Np63α-expressing cells, no statistically significant increase in spontaneous pulmonary metastases was observed for AsPC1 or HPAFII, however, pulmonary metastases were enriched for ∆Np63 expression as compared to established primary tumors, including expression of endogenous ∆Np63 in the mCherry control. Increased resistance to irinotecan chemotherapy was observed in ∆Np63α + HPAFII, yet treatment selected for ∆Np63-negative cells in both HPAFII and ASPC1. In summary, our data show that PDAC metastases are enriched for basal subtype, but chemotherapy treatment does not preferentially select for basal-type cells.

title: Cellular proximity and conditional coordination in the colorectal and pancreatic tumor microenvironment: a patient-level analysis of multiplexed imaging
abstract: Immune cells in the tumor microenvironment are organized, and in colorectal and pancreatic cancer their arrangement around the tumor epithelium carries prognostic information. Multiplexed tissue imaging records the position and phenotype of every cell in a section, and studies of such images now routinely report that two cell types are spatially associated. However, the summaries behind these reports answer different questions. A proximity statistic asks whether two cell types lie close together more often than expected by chance. A conditional network asks whether their local densities rise and fall together once the other cell types are held fixed. The two can disagree, because every cell type is abundant where tissue is cell-dense and because the images of one patient are repeated measurements of that patient. We asked how epithelial and immune cells are organized in two settings: colorectal cancer with a Crohn's-like reaction (CLR) or diffuse inflammatory infiltration (DII), in 140 CODEX images from 35 patients, and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) against its precursor, intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm (IPMN), in 207 multiplex immunofluorescence images from 141 patients. We developed a patient-level analysis that keeps proximity, recurrent local composition and conditional coordination as separate quantities, tests conditional organization as a function of local epithelial density within each section, checks before every conditional estimate that the two cell types are disjoint sets of cells observed together in enough images, and calibrates each conclusion by patient-label permutation, cellularity adjustment under two definitions, spatial-scale perturbation and fully nested leave-one-patient-out prediction. In colorectal cancer, the conditional association between epithelial and myeloid density turned negative with local epithelial density about four times faster in DII than in CLR (difference $-0.0553$ per quartile; 95% CI, $-0.0833$ to $-0.0273$; patient-label familywise $P=0.006$), with no accompanying difference in proximity. In the pancreas, cytotoxic and helper T cells were closer together in PDAC than in IPMN at every scale examined ($q\leq0.023$), whereas their conditional association differed between the two diseases under only one of the two cellularity definitions. Recurrent neighborhoods carried the most patient-level information in colorectal cancer (AUC 0.794) and combined spatial features in the pancreas (AUC 0.771). Pancreatic epithelial--immune and regulatory T-cell quantities could not be estimated from these cores and are reported as such. The analysis is implemented in the R package spatialMIFtools, available at https://github.com/sagnikbhadury/spatialMIFtools.

title: Self-extending DNA recording with stochastic and programmed writing
abstract: Recording cellular histories requires new information to accumulate without erasing earlier records. Here we introduce Infinite Printer, a CRISPR recording architecture that couples self-extension to regeneration of a writable terminal context. A self-targeting prime-editing guide RNA (stpegRNA) directs repeat extension, while base editing generates diversity in situ without a separate insertion template for each character state. Earlier sequence remains upstream of the renewed terminus, linking substrate growth with record retention. Auxiliary pegRNAs specify payloads within a write-renew-write architecture. After three rounds of payload input, 4,436 distinct complete CCA-based records contained identities from all three pools. Longer AC/AT records retained shared upstream marks, and full-length sequence analysis resolved additional endpoint distinctions. Joint single-cell readout recovered 1,549 distinct records and 7,669 combinations across 12,302 transcriptome-linked cell labels from a single stpegRNA design. Spatial-transcriptomic readout recovered spacer records at 11,330 capture spots, linking record content to tissue coordinates and gene-expression profiles. Infinite Printer unites substrate renewal, sequence diversification and programmed writing with cell- and tissue-linked readout, providing a foundation for future lineage recording across large cell populations during mammalian development.
